2.59.m: Viṣṇu said: / Having accomplished [visits to] all the sacred places, Kṛkala set out towards home / accompanied by a caravan, filled with great joy.
Thus he constantly reflected: 'My worldly existence has borne fruit; / my ancestors, fully satisfied, will attain heaven, not otherwise.'
Meanwhile, [someone] in visible form, having bound his ancestors, / said directly before him: 'There is no supreme merit for you.'
One of divine form and huge body spoke these words to Kṛkala: / 'You have no fruit of the sacred places; you have made this exertion entirely in vain.
You obtain satisfaction only for yourself; there is no supreme merit for you.' / Having heard this, the vaiśya Kṛkala was afflicted with sorrow:
'Who are you that speak thus? Why are my grandfathers bound? / Tell me the cause of that: through the power of which fault?'
'Why is there no fruit of the sacred places? How is my pilgrimage in vain? / Tell me everything clearly, if you know.'
Dharma said: / He who sets out having abandoned his pure, most meritorious wife— / all the fruit of his merit becomes useless, not otherwise.
He who sets out on a righteous deed, abandoning even that wife / devoted to virtuous conduct, holy, intent on pious vows, devoted to her husband, virtuous, and fond of merit—
all the dharma performed by him becomes useless, not otherwise.
Devoted to all proper conduct, noble, intent on the means of dharma, / constantly devoted to her husband, always fond of wisdom—
in whose house there is a wife possessing such qualities, holy and a great faithful wife, / the gods of great splendour reside permanently in his home.
Dwelling within the house, the ancestors desire his welfare; / the sacred rivers such as the Gaṅgā and the oceans are there, not otherwise.
In whose house there is a holy faithful wife devoted to truth, / sacrifices, cows, and sages are there, not otherwise.
All the sacred places and various meritorious [sites] / abide there through union with a wife, all these, not otherwise.
Householder life comes to be through union with a virtuous wife; / there is no second dharma superior to householder life on the surface of the earth.
The house of a householder is sacred, endowed with truth and merit; / O vaiśya, it consists of all sacred places and is accompanied by all the gods.
Depending upon the householder stage of life, all living beings live; / I do not see any other stage of life as excellent as that.
Mantras, the agnihotra fire, the gods, all eternal dharmas, / and practices of charity proceed in the home of the man
who [has a wife]; but the house of one destitute of a wife becomes like a forest; / sacrifices do not succeed, nor do charities of various kinds.
For a man destitute of a wife, not even a great vow succeeds, / nor any righteous deeds, nor various meritorious acts.
There is no sacred place equal to a wife for accomplishing dharma; / listen, for a householder there is no other dharma in the three worlds.
Where a wife is, there is home, even for a man, not otherwise; / whether in a village or in a forest, she is the means of accomplishing all dharma.
There is no sacred place equal to a wife, there is no happiness equal to a wife, / there is no merit equal to a wife for deliverance and benefit.
O lowest of men, you who went forth abandoning a faithful wife endowed with dharma, / having forsaken your home and your dharma, where is the fruit of your dharma?
Since the offering of śrāddha was made by you at the sacred places without her, / through that fault, indeed, your earlier grandfathers have been bound.
You are a thief, and these are thieves, who being intensely greedy ate / the food of the śrāddha offered by you without her in this manner.
When a good son endowed with faith gives the gift of śrāddha / with the rice-ball offered alongside his wife, I shall tell his merit:
Just as the satisfaction of men arises from drinking nectar, / so it does for the ancestors through śrāddha; I speak the truth, the truth.
The wife is the mistress of the householder's life and of dharma; / she was deceived by you, O fool, and your act of theft was in vain.
These grandfathers are thieves, by whom [food] was eaten without her; / if a wife cooks food with her own hand, resembling nectar,
the ancestors partake of that food alone with joyful minds; / by that alone they attain satisfaction, and they become well-pleased.
Therefore, without a wife, dharma does not succeed for a man; / there is no sacred place equal to a wife that bestows a good destination upon men.
And whatever religious duty is performed without a wife becomes completely fruitless."

2.60.m: Kṛkala said: / "How will my spiritual success come about? How will the deliverance of my ancestors occur? / Tell me this at length, O Dharmarāja, right now."
Dharma said: / "Go home, O fortunate one; without you, she suffers grief. / Console your wife Sukalā, who walks the path of dharma.
Having gone home, perform the offering of ancestral rites with her own hand; / remembering the sacred places of pilgrimage, worship the foremost among the gods.
The spiritual success accomplished by pilgrimage will surely become yours. / But in this world, whoever wishes to practice dharma without a wife,
he should abandon householder life and wander through the forest alone; / he becomes fruitless in this world, and the gods do not esteem him.
Sacrifices attain success only when a housewife is in the home; / alone, he is not capable of accomplishing religious duty and prosperity."
Viṣṇu said: / Having spoken thus to that merchant, Dharma went as he had come; / and Kṛkala, righteous in soul, set out toward his own home.
Having reached his home, the intelligent one saw that devoted wife; / with that caravan leader, the wise man reached his own place.
Seeing her husband, skilled in dharma, arrived, / she then performed an auspicious and sacred rite at her husband's homecoming.
That righteous-souled man related the deeds of Dharma. / Hearing her husband's joy-bringing words, the noble woman,
having praised the words of Dharma, consented to it accordingly. / Viṣṇu said: / Then that merchant Kṛkala, together with her,
faithfully performed a most sacred śrāddha, remaining in the temple of the deity. / The ancestors, gods, and Gandharvas arrived in aerial cars.
They, the great-souled sages, praised the couple, / as did I, Brahmā, and Maheśvara along with the Goddess.
All the gods along with the Gandharvas arrived in aerial cars; / indeed, I, then Brahmā, and Maheśvara along with the Goddess,
and all the gods accompanied by Gandharvas were pleased by her truthfulness. / And they spoke to the two great-souled ones, who knew dharma and were learned in truth:
"Together with your wife, may good befall you: choose a boon, O you of noble vows!" / Kṛkala said: / "By the influence of whose merit and austerity, O foremost among the gods,
have you come to grant a boon to me together with my wife?" / Indra said: / "This virtuous, fortunate Sukalā possesses lovely auspiciousness.
We are pleased with her truthfulness and wish to grant you a boon." / And in brief, that previous account was related [to him].
Hearing the greatness of her conduct, her husband rejoiced. / Together with her, that righteous-souled man, his eyes agitated with joy,
bowed down to all the deities and spoke again and again: / "If the three eternal gods, who are of great fortune,
and other holy ṛṣis are pleased, having shown compassion upon me: / birth after birth, let me have such devotion to the gods;
may I have delight in dharma and truth, through your favor. / Furthermore, together with my wife and with my forefathers,
I wish to go to the world of Viṣṇu, O gods, if you of great might are pleased." / The gods said: / "So be it, O fortunate one; all this shall indeed come to pass."
Then they rained down flowers upon the two of them, O king. / Then they sang a most holy, charming song in lovely tunes.
Gandharvas who knew the truth of song and hosts of Apsarases danced. / Then the gods along with the Gandharvas, O best of kings,
having granted the boon and praising the devoted wife, went to their respective abodes. / The sacred pilgrimage of the wife has been fully recounted; I shall tell you of something else.
This entire unexcelled sacred narrative has been recounted to you. / A man who hears it, O king, is freed from all sins.
If a woman hears this excellent narrative of Sukalā with faith, / she is never parted from good fortune, truth, sons, or grandsons.
She rejoices with wealth and grain, and becomes happy together with her husband. / She will be a devoted wife birth after birth; it cannot be otherwise.
A brāhmaṇa becomes learned in the Vedas, and a kṣatriya becomes victorious; / wealth and grain will surely be in the house of a vaiśya, without a doubt.
He becomes a knower of dharma, O king, endowed with good conduct, and happy; / a śūdra attains happiness and prospers with sons and grandsons.
Abundant fortune arises, adorned with wealth and grain.

2.61.m: Vena said: / "The sacred pilgrimage of the wife has been declared the supreme among all holy places; / relate now the sacred pilgrimage of the parents, the ultimate means of deliverance for sons."
Viṣṇu said: / "In the great sacred place Kurukṣetra, there was a brāhmaṇa named Kuṇḍala; / Sukarmā was the virtuous son of the noble Kuṇḍala.
His parents were very elderly, knowers of dharma, learned in the scriptures; / both of these great-souled ones were sorely afflicted by old age.
He then rendered service to both of them with supreme devotion, / knowing dharma, endowed with love, day and night without ceasing.
From him, his father, he studied the Vedas and numerous scriptures; / devoted to all proper conduct, capable, knowing dharma, loving knowledge.
He himself massaged the limbs of his two elders, / and washed their feet, and attended to their bathing and feeding.
Out of devotion and by his very nature, he became absorbed in meditating upon them; / O lord of kings, he carried out attendance upon his mother and father."
Sūta said: / At that current time, O best of kings, / there was a brāhmaṇa named Pippala, belonging to the noble Kaśyapa line.
He performed austerities, abstaining from food, self-conquered, free from malice, / endowed with compassion, charity, and self-restraint, having conquered desire and anger.
Having gone to the Daśāraṇya forest, wise and devoted to knowledge and peace, / restraining all his sense faculties, the noble-minded one performed austerities.
By the power of his austerity, creatures there, free from hostility, / lived as if in the golden age, as though born from one womb.
Seeing that austerity of his, the sages fell into wonder: / 'Such austerity has not been practiced by anyone, as this sage practices.'
And the gods, headed by Indra, fell into supreme wonder: / 'Oh, how intense is his austerity, his tranquility, and his restraint of the senses!
Free from change, free from agitation, devoid of desire and anger, / enduring cold, wind, and heat, he stands like a mountain.
Averse to sense-objects, steadfast, having transcended the mind's grasping, / the best of the twice-born hears no sound from anyone whatsoever.'
Having reached such a steady posture, standing with one-pointed mind, / absorbed in meditation on Brahman, his lotus-face filled with bliss,
having become like stone or wood, motionless, he stood like a mountain; / and he appeared like a pillar, firmly fixed, devoted to dharma.
His body was emaciated by austerity, exceedingly full of faith, free from envy; / in this way, one thousand years passed for that wise sage.
A heap consisting of a mass of earth was made by numerous ants; / upon him, as their own abode, [rose] an anthill of huge size.
Standing within the interior of the anthill, he stood as though turned to stone; / in this way that brāhmaṇa Pippala practiced immense austerity.
The best of twice-borns was surrounded on all sides by black serpents; / fraught with fierce venom, they bit that sage of dread energy.
Reaching the vital parts of his body, their venom could not penetrate him; / by the fiery energy of that twice-born, the snakes then became calm.
From his body of blazing energy arose flames of light, / manifold in form, seen repeatedly and distinctly,
fiercer than fire itself, of such a kind, O best among men! / Just as the sun, having entered the belly of a cloud, shines with its rays,
so the brahmin Pippala, seated in the anthill, shone with fiery power. / Angrily the snakes bit that sage with their fangs;
yet from the tips of their fangs they could not pierce his skin, O best of kings. / Thus, while he was practicing austerity for a thousand years,
there passed away, O king of kings, for that great-souled sage / who persevered during the three divisions of the day through cold, rain, and heat,
the time, O great king, of the high-souled Pippala; / likewise, that great soul subsisted on air alone.
Three thousand years passed while he practiced austerities. / Then upon his head a shower of flowers was poured by the gods of old.
"You are a knower of Brahman, O fortunate one; you are a knower of dharma, without a doubt; / you are full of all knowledge, born [to it] by your own action.
Whatever desire you wish for, that very thing you will attain, not otherwise; / you will become one whose every wish is fulfilled of his own accord."
Hearing that momentous speech, the high-minded Pippala, / having bowed to all the deities with his neck bent in devotion,
overcome with great joy, replied with these words: / "So that this entire universe might become subject to my control,
make it so, O lords of the gods, and let me become a Vidyādhara!" / Having spoken thus, that wise man paused, O best of kings.
"So be it!" the gods then said to the best of twice-borns. / Having granted the boon to that great-souled one, the blessed ones departed.
When those gods had gone, the excellent brahmin Pippala / constantly cultivated brahminhood and thought of bringing the universe under his control.
From then on, O king of kings, the excellent brahmin Pippala, / having attained the rank of a Vidyādhara, moving wherever he wished, was glorified.
Thus that twice-born Pippala, having attained the rank of a Vidyādhara, / became a lord in the world of the gods, proficient in all sacred treatises.
Once, however, the mighty Pippala reflected: / "The whole universe must be in my power, [for] an excellent boon was granted to me."
To put it to the test, that foremost among twice-borns set about: / whomever he thought of subduing, that very one he brought under control.
When this proof had thus occurred, he thought in his mind: / "There is no second person in the world equal to me, the best of men!"
Sūta said: / While the high-souled Pippala was thinking thus, / having perceived his mental state, a crane said to him;
standing on the bank of the lake, O king, with a melodious sound, endowed with distinct syllables, / with an utterance full of elegance, he said to Pippala:
"Why do you harbor such pride, [imagining yourself] supreme? / I do not consider that power of universal subjugation to belong to you alone.
This matter of what is submissive or unsubmissive is praised as recent; / you do not know the ancient [truth], Pippala, for you are dull of intellect.
Just because three thousand years of austerity / have been performed by you, why do you vainly show pride, O twice-born?
The son of Kuṇḍala, the steadfast and wise Sukarman, free of affliction— / the whole world was subject to him, both compliant and uncompliant; hear [of him] now.
That wise one knows both the recent and the ancient; / there is no great sage in the world equal to him; hear, O Pippala!
You are not equal to Sukarman, the son of Kuṇḍala. / No gift was given by him, nor was [esoteric] knowledge meditated upon;
sacrifices with offerings and the like were never performed by him; / he went on no pilgrimage, nor [did he engage in] worship of fire.
When did he ever perform, O twice-born, the highest service to dharma? / Moving at will, possessing knowledge, he is ever a friend to his father and mother,
rich in Vedic study, skilled in the meaning of all treatises. / Such as the knowledge of that boy Sukarman is,
such knowledge you do not have; you bear pride in vain!" / Pippala said: / "Who are you, reproaching me in the form of a bird?
Why do you disparage my knowledge, and of what kind is the ancient [truth]? / Tell me that in detail; how could there be knowledge in you?
The whole state of the recent and of the ancient now, / declare it, O best of birds, along with knowledge in full detail.
Are you Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Rudra?" / The crane said: / "There is no disposition toward austerity in you, nor is there any fruit of it.
Hear now about the austerity not fully mastered by you: / such virtue as belongs to the son of Kuṇḍala, even though he is a boy,
just so, knowledge has not been attained by you, nor that state grasped. / Going from here, ask him about my form, O best of twice-borns.
That virtuous one will speak all knowledge to you." / Viṣṇu said: / Having heard all that which was spoken by the crane,
he departed swiftly for the Daśāraṇya, the great hermitage.

2.62.m: Viṣṇu said: / Having gone to the hermitage of Kuṇḍala, crowded with truth and dharma, / he then saw Sukarman devoted to his father and mother,
that high-souled one serving his parents, of true valor, / possessing great beauty, great splendor, endowed with great knowledge.
He saw him seated at the feet of his mother and father, / endowed with great devotion, tranquil, a great treasure of all knowledge.
And by the son of Kuṇḍala, the great-souled Sukarman, / seeing Pippala of great intellect arrived at the doorway,
rising quickly from his seat, welcoming respect was made: / "Come, O fortunate one, high-minded Vidyādhara!"
The wise one offered him a seat, foot-water, and respectful offering: / "Are you free from obstacles, O deeply wise one? Do you fare well?"
And he inquired after the health of Pippala who had arrived: / "For what reason you have come today, all that I shall tell [you].
For as long as three thousand years, austerity / was practiced by you, O fortunate one, and from the gods you obtained a boon;
power of subjugation was obtained by you, and likewise freedom of movement; / puffed up by that, you do not understand, and you bear pride in vain.
Seeing all your behavior, the great-souled crane / spoke my name and my unsurpassed knowledge."
Pippala said: / "Who was that crane who addressed me on the riverbank, O twice-born, / saying, 'He will speak all knowledge to you'? Who was that lord, that ruler?"
Sukarman said: / "The crane who spoke to you on the riverbank, / know him to be Brahmā, of great knowledge, the supreme lord.
What else do you ask? Tell me, and I will declare it to you." / Viṣṇu said: / Thus addressed, that righteous Sukarman, O son of the king—
Pippala said: / "'The entire world is subject to you'—so we have heard on earth. / Therefore show that wonder to me, O twice-born, with effort!"
“Behold now a miracle—the reason behind what is submissive and not submissive.” / That righteous Sukarmā said to Pippala:
Then Sukarmā remembered the gods to produce conviction: / Indra and the other world guardians, and the gods headed by Agni.
Summoned, they gathered, along with various Vidyādharas. / Then the gods headed by Agni said to Sukarmā:
“Why have you remembered us, O Brahmin? Speak the reason for this matter.” / Sukarmā said: “This Pippala, a Vidyādhara, has arrived here.
He speaks to me, O Brahmin, about the reason for things being submissive and not submissive. / You have been summoned for the conviction of this great-souled one.
Go each to your own abode,” he said to the gods. / Then those gods said to Sukarmā of great intellect:
“The sight of us, O Brahmin, does not become fruitless; it is a boon. / Choose a boon, good fortune to you, whatever pleases your mind.
We will grant it to you, there is no doubt.” Thus said the best of the gods. / Having bowed to those gods with devotion, that best of the twice-born requested:
“Grant unwavering, excellent devotion endowed with love, O lords of the gods, / and for my mother and father, always. That indeed is the unsurpassed boon.
May my father go to the world of Viṣṇu—this is the highest boon; / likewise my mother, O lords of the gods. I ask for no other boon.”
The gods said: “You are devoted to your parents, O best of Brahmins; because of your devotion, O twice-born, / O Sukarmā, hear our word: we are always pleased with you.”
Having spoken thus, the gods departed to heaven, O son of the king. / All this sovereign power was demonstrated before him by him.
Pippala also saw the wonderful and exceedingly marvelous sight. / That righteous one said to Pippala, the son of Kuṇḍala:
“This is the lower form; what is the higher form like? / Tell of the power of both, O best of speakers.”
Sukarmā said: “I will tell you the mark of the higher form, / by which the worlds, Indra and the rest, with mobile and immobile beings, rejoice.
He alone is the Lord of the universe, all-pervading, the pervasive Master; / his form has never been seen by any yogin at all.
The scripture speaks thus, as if hesitant to describe him: / ‘Without hands, feet, or nose, earless, devoid of a mouth,
he sees every deed done by the inhabitants of the three worlds. / Devoid of ears, he hears what they have said, providing true witness.
Deprived of locomotion, he travels; he is indeed seen everywhere. / Devoid of hands he grasps; devoid of feet he runs.
Everywhere he is seen, O Brahmin, all-pervading, devoid of feet. / Him the lords of the gods and the sages who perceive reality do not see,
yet he sees all of them situated in the realm of truth and falsehood— / pervasive, spotless, perfected, bestower of perfections, leader of all,
whom the great yogin Vyāsa, skilled in dharma and artha, knows. / He is an embodiment of splendor, like space, of a single color, infinite.’
The scripture definitely declares this pure form. / Vyāsa knows, and Mārkaṇḍeya knows that state.
I shall describe the lower form; listen with a single-pointed mind: / when the Soul of beings, having withdrawn [all], goes forth alone,
taking his bed upon the waters, resting on the seat of the coils of Śeṣa, / relying upon him, Janārdana sleeps alone for a long time.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, tormented by the darkness in the water, / seeking a place, yogic in soul, grew weary from wandering.
While wandering, he saw the one who lies upon the couch of Śeṣa, / resembling ten million suns, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing a divine garland and garment, the all-pervading Lord, / who had entered into the sleep of yoga, lovely, holding the conch, discus, and mace.
There was a fortunate woman, resembling a heap of black collyrium, / her face dreadful with fangs, of terrifying form, O best of the twice-born.
That foremost of sages, the great sage, was told by her: ‘Do not fear!’ / A vast lotus leaf, five leagues long,
upon that leaf Mārkaṇḍeya was placed by the great goddess: / ‘Even though Keśava is asleep, you have no fear here.’
That lord of yogins said to her: ‘Who are you, O beautiful lady? / In this desolate [realm], you alone are thriving.’
Thus questioned by the sage, the goddess respectfully said, O Brahmin: / ‘He who sleeps on the couch of the serpent’s coils is Keśava.
I am his Vaiṣṇava power, called here the Night of Time. / Know me thus, O best of Brahmins, endowed with all magical illusion.
In the Purāṇas I am called Mahāmāyā for the delusion of the universe.’ / Having spoken thus, that goddess disappeared, O Pippala.
When the goddess had departed, as Mārkaṇḍeya watched, / a lotus with the luster of gold arose from his navel.
From that was born the grand ancestor of the world, Brahmā of great splendor; / from him were born all the worlds, mobile and immobile.
the guardians of the worlds beginning with Indra, and the gods headed by Agni. / This immanent form was indeed shown by me, O king.
This immanent form is [visible], while the transcendent one is without support. / Whenever he shows a body, they take the forms of bodies.
All worlds beginning with Brahmā are indeed immanent, O Pippala; / immanent are these worlds that exist in the three worlds.
He, the transcendent Self of beings, is what yogins behold clearly: / the supreme abode having the nature of liberation, identical with the supreme Brahman,
unmanifest, imperishable, the Swan, pure, endowed with supernatural powers. / What the form of the transcendent is, O Vidyādhara, [has been set] before you.
All this has thus been declared by me; what else shall I tell you? / Pippala said: Whence has this great knowledge arisen in you, O man of good vows?
Knowing the immanent state and likewise the transcendent state, / the supreme knowledge of the threefold world thus abides in you alone.
I do not see the supreme culmination of asceticism [in you], O man of good vows. / Have you performed sacrifices, officiating for others, pilgrimages to sacred fords, or asceticism?
Tell that power in this way: by what means do you possess all knowledge? / Sukarma said: I do not know asceticism, nor have I emaciated my body.
Sacrifices, officiating for others, or undertaking pilgrimages to sacred fords—I know not; / meditation and the meritorious time arising from good deeds have not been practiced by me.
One thing clearly I know: the worship of father and mother. / With my hands I continually [attend] both parents.
I myself perform the meritorious washing of the feet; / and likewise massaging of the limbs, bathing, and meals.
Absorbed in meditation at the three junctions of the day, I accomplish [it] day after day; / and the water from the feet of both mother and father, day after day,
I receive with devotional disposition, and I worship them with genuine love. / For as long as my two teachers are living, O Pippala,
for so long indeed does incomparable benefit arise for me. / At the three junctions of the day I worship these two with a pure heart.
I roam freely in playful movement, O Pippala! / What need have I of other asceticism? What need of emaciating the body?
What need have I now of pilgrimages to holy fords or other meritorious acts? / The fruit that is attained from all sacrifices, O twice-born,
that fruit has been seen by me through service to the father, / and service to the mother likewise brings the supreme destination to sons.
It is the all-in-all among all deeds, the essence in the threefold world. / A son attains a world even through service to the mother.
Likewise, in service to the father, great merit arises. / The Gaṅgā is there, the sacred ford Gayā is there, and Puṣkara is right there,
wherever mother and father dwell for a son—there is no doubt. / The other diverse, meritorious sacred fords—
all these accrue to a son from service to the father. / From service to his father comes the fruit of giving and asceticism
for a good son, O brahmin; other religious duty turns to mere toil. / From service to the father, a son obtains unexcelled merit.
It is the entirety of one's own duty, both here and in the hereafter. / When his own mother and father, the two venerable teachers, are alive,
and one serves them as a son, hear the meritorious fruit of that! / The gods are pleased with him, and the sages affectionate toward merit.
The three worlds are indeed pleased by service to the father in this world. / Whoever daily washes the feet of his mother and father,
for him a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day. / Whoever feeds his father and mother with meritorious, sweet food and drink,
daily and with devotion, I shall declare his merit: / the fruit of the horse sacrifice arises for that son.
By betel, clothing, drinks, and meals, / and with devotion and pure food, by whoever the two venerable elders are worshipped,
he becomes all-knowing, and he attains fame and renown. / Beholding father and mother, a son should converse with joy;
treasures, well-pleased with him, dwell in his house; / cows are affectionate toward the son, bestowing happiness at all times.

2.63.m: Sukarma said: And, O best of the twice-born, when drops of water fall / upon all the limbs of a son from both parents as they are bathed,
a bath equal to all sacred fords is fully attained by that son. / Fallen, impaired, aged, incapable in all activities,
diseased, leprous—the son who attends upon such a father, / and upon a mother in like condition—I shall declare his merit.
Viṣṇu becomes pleased in heart with him; of this there is no doubt. / He goes to the Vaiṣṇava realm, which is unattainable even by yogins.
When the two parents are crippled, wretched, aged—these two teachers— / and struck by a great disease, if an evil-minded son abandons them,
that son goes to a frightful hell crowded with worms. / When called by the two aged teachers here at that moment,
if he being a son does not go, I shall declare his sin: / that fool becomes a village swine feeding on feces, without a doubt,
for a thousand births, and then he is born as a dog. / When the aged mother and father are staying in the son's house,
the son who eats food himself without first feeding them / feeds on urine and feces for a thousand births.
That sinner becomes a black serpent for two hundred births. / Disregarding an aged mother and father, if he acts [arrogantly],
that wicked one becomes a crocodile for even a hundred crores of births. / If a son reviles those two with harsh words,
that sinner becomes a tiger, and afterward is born as a bear. / The wicked-minded son who does not show respect to his mother and father
shall dwell in Kuṃbhīpāka for as long as a thousand yugas. / There is no sacred ford equal to a mother, nor any equal to a father for sons,
for salvation and for welfare, both here and in the hereafter. / Therefore, O greatly wise one, I worship the father as a god,
and the mother as a god, all the gods; thus I have become an accomplished yogin. / By the grace of mother and father, supreme knowledge has arisen.
This entire threefold world has come under my control. / I know the immanent state of this great-souled god,
and likewise the transcendent state of that same Vāsudeva, O highly intelligent one. / All knowledge has arisen through the grace of father and mother.
What wise man does not worship his father and mother? / Of what use are the Vedas, studied with their limbs and secondary limbs,
endowed with the scriptures of revelation, O brahmins, if the father is not worshipped by him? / If the mother is not worshipped by him, his Vedas are useless.
What is the use of sacrifices and asceticism, O brahmin, of gifts and worship? / It all comes to vanity for him by whom the mother is not worshipped,
and by whom the father is not worshipped, while living and staying in the house. / This alone is duty for a son, this is the sacred ford among men in this world;
this alone is liberation for a son, and the auspicious fruit of birth; / this alone is sacrifice for a son, and indeed gift-giving, without a doubt.
One should constantly worship the father with devotion, disposition, and intentness; / for him, all that which was mentioned before has been realized.
The fruit of giving and of a sacred ford is attained by him, without a doubt; / the fruit of sacrifice is also obtained by him who has attended upon his mother.

By whomsoever the father has been served daily with great devotion,
all his merit-yielding actions, sacrifices and the like, are completely accomplished.

For this reason, the Dharmaśāstra heard by me is properly understood:
a son should indeed constantly be dedicated to devotion toward his father, O Pippala.

Hear formerly how, when his father was pleased, happiness was attained by King Yadu,
and how great sin was incurred when the father was angered.

And by Ruru, the Paurava, when he was cursed by his father on earth.
Thus knowledge was obtained by me, because those two were served.
And by their grace, the unsurpassed fruit was attained.

2.64.m:
Pippala said:
How by Yadu, through the disposition of his father’s grace, was supreme happiness
attained and well enjoyed? Tell me that in detail.

And why does Ruru suffer the effect of sin, O best of the twice-born?
Tell me everything in detail, O son of Kuṇḍala.

Sukarma said:
Let it be heard! I will recount the sin-destroying account
of the highly meritorious Nahuṣa and of the great-souled Yayāti.

Born from the lunar dynasty, Nahuṣa was lord of the earth,
and he performed numerous unequaled righteous deeds of giving.

He performed an excellent hundred horse sacrifices,
and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, as well as diverse other sacrifices.

By the power of his own merit, he attained the world of Indra;
he made his son, endowed with virtues of righteousness, the protector of the subjects,

Yayāti, endowed with truth, possessing righteous valor, and highly intelligent.
The king went to the position of Indra, and his son [was established] in his own position.

Yayāti, endowed with truth, protected the subjects righteously;
he himself personally inspected those deeds of his subjects.

Knowing dharma, he had sacrifices performed after hearing the unsurpassed dharma;
he performed all sacrifices, pilgrimages, and the merit of giving.

The wise prince then ruled the kingdom with truth and righteousness
for as long as eighty thousand years.

So much time passed for that great-souled Yayāti.
And he had four sons, of his own vigor, strength, and valor.

I shall declare their names; listen with single-minded attention:
his eldest son was named Ruru, of great strength;

the second was named Puru; another, the third, was Kuru;
and the fourth son of the king was named Yadu, righteous-souled.

Thus there were four sons of that great-souled Yayāti,
equal to their father in valor, in splendor, and also in manly courage.

Thus the kingdom was governed righteously by that Yayāti;
his fame and renown became abundant throughout the three worlds.

Viṣṇu said:
Once indeed, the best of the twice-born, Nārada, the son of Brahmā,
went to the world of Indra, O King, to see Purandara.

Then the thousand-eyed god saw the priest approaching,
equal in luster to fire, omniscient and learned in wisdom.

Honored with the madhuparka offering and the like, his neck bowed in devotion,
[Indra] seated him on a holy seat and questioned that best of sages.

Indra said:
Why is your arrival today, and for what purpose have you come here?
What very pleasing thing, O priest, O great sage, shall I do for you today?

Nārada said:
O king of the gods, all has been done with devotion, and whatever was said [is accepted].
I am satisfied, O highly wise one; I will answer your question.

I have just now arrived at your mansion from the earthly world;
I have come to seek you out after having seen the son of Nahuṣa.

Indra said:
What king always protects the subjects with truth and righteousness,
endowed with all virtues, learned in scripture, possessor of knowledge, virtuous?

What king is there on earth, knower of the Veda, dear to brāhmaṇas,
devoted to brāhmaṇas, knowing the Veda, heroic, sacrificing, generous, and truly devoted?

Nārada said:
The powerful son of Nahuṣa is endowed with these qualities,
by whose truth and valor all the worlds are established.

In the earthly world, Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa is like you;
you are in heaven, and he on the surface of the earth, increasing prosperity.

Superior to his father, the great king Yayāti, lord of the earth,
performed a hundred horse sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeyas.

Various forms of gifts were given by him with devotion:
hundreds of thousands of cows and hundreds of millions of cows.

He performed ten-million-fold fire offerings and hundred-thousand-fold fire offerings as well;
and he gave gifts such as land and others to brāhmaṇas.

By him the entire essence of righteousness was truly upheld;
such is the son of Nahuṣa, Yayāti, endowed with virtues.

For eighty thousand years that best of kings
ruled the kingdom with truth, like you here in heaven.

Sukarma said:
Having thus heard from Nārada, that lord of sages,
the wise lord of the gods reflected, terrified of [the king’s] adherence to dharma.

“Formerly, by the power of a hundred sacrifices, Nahuṣa
attained my position of Indra; the hero formerly became the king of the gods.

By the power of Śacī’s intellect, he became fallen from that rank;
this great king is like that, equal in valor to his father.

He will attain the position of Indra—there is no doubt here, no hesitation.
By some means or other, I must bring that king to heaven.”
Thus indeed reflected the lord of the gods, frightened on that account, / out of great fear of the protector of the earth, the best of kings, Yayāti.

Then the king of the gods sent a messenger to bring him,
[and] Nahuṣa’s celestial chariot, granting all desires,

accompanied by the chariot [with] the charioteer named Mātali.
Mātali indeed went there where the son of Nahuṣa was staying,

dispatched by the king of the gods to bring the highly intelligent one.
Present in his assembly, just as Indra shines,

so Yayāti, the righteous-souled, shone in his own assembly.
To that great-souled king adorned with truth, he spoke:

Whatever the king of the gods says, do all that with a cheerful mind:
you must come, O king, to the world of Indra, not otherwise.

Relinquishing the kingdom to your son, having performed the excellent final sacrifice,
[come where] King Ila of great splendor dwells, O son of Nahuṣa,

where Purūravas of great valor, Vipracitti of great mind,
and Śibi dwell; right there King Manu Ikṣvāku,

the wise one named Sagara, and your father Nahuṣa,
Ṛtavīrya, Kṛtajña, and Śaṃtanu of noble mind,

Bharata, Yuvanāśva, and King Kārtavīrya;
having performed sacrifices in many ways, the kings rejoice in heaven.

And other kings dedicated to sacrificial actions,
all those, through their own deeds, rejoice in heaven with Indra.

You, moreover, know all dharma and are established in all dharmas;
rejoice together with Śakra in the heavenly world, O lord of the earth.

Yayāti said:
What is that deed done by me, for which this request to me
from Indra, the king of the gods, [has been made]? Tell me all that.

Mātali said:
Because for eighty thousand years, O King,
deeds of giving, merit, and the like were thoroughly accomplished by you through sacrifices,
[Mātali said:] ‘Go to heaven, O great king, by your own action, O protector of the earth; / make friendship with the king of the gods, go to the abode of the gods.
Abandon this body composed of five elements on the earth, O high-minded one; / assuming a divine form, enjoy pleasures conforming to your mind.
In whatever manner sacrifices, gifts, and asceticism were performed by you on earth, / in that same manner the pleasures of heaven present themselves, O ruler of men.’
Yayāti said: ‘By which body good deeds and bad deeds are accomplished on earth, / O Mātali, how, having abandoned that, could one go to the earned world?’
Mātali said: ‘Wherever this body composed of five elements was acquired, O king, / abandoning it right there, they go to that [world] by means of a divine [body] alone.
All other human beings, performers of sin and merit, / they too, having abandoned the body, go downward or upward.’
Yayāti said: ‘Men, having produced good and bad deeds with a body composed of five elements, / indeed go downward or upward, O Mātali.
What is the distinction, O knower of dharma, that one should abandon the body on the earth? / Does the fall of the body happen through the power of sin or merit?
An example is seen, O Sūta, visibly in the realm of mortals; / I do not see any special increase from sin and merit.
By which body a mortal man earns truth, dharma, and other deeds, / why should he cast that very one away?
The self and the body—these two are both in the form of friends. / Having abandoned the body, his friend, the self goes away with certainty.’
Mātali said: ‘What you have said is true, O king: having abandoned the body, he goes; / and he, the self, has no connection together with the body,
because this [body] has dissolution as its nature, its joints always worn out, / oppressed by old age, and always corrupted by diseases.
Broken by the defects of old age, it does not wish to stay here; / becoming bewildered and agitated, the living soul abandons it and departs.
By truth, virtues of dharma, gifts, observances and self-restraints, / by sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice, by sacred fords, and likewise by restraints,
by good merits and other good deeds, old age is not held back at all; / and through sins, O great king, it dissolves the body itself.’
Yayāti said: ‘Why did old age arise? Why does it torment the body? / You ought to tell me in detail, O best of beings.’” }  ],
Mātali said: / Look, I shall describe to you the primary cause of old age, / and how it arises within the body, O best of kings.
The body consists of the five elements; it is supported by the five sense-objects. / When the self abandons it, O king, that body is burnt away.
Kindled by fire, it blazes with bodily fluid, O king; / from that, smoke is generated, and from smoke clouds are born.
Waters issue from the cloud; from the waters the earth is fashioned; / that virtuous water comes just like a menstruating woman.
From that is produced smell; from smell comes taste, O best of kings; / from taste food arises, and from food semen, without a doubt.
From semen indeed the body is born; and the body is misshapen. / Just as the earth produces smells and ranges upon the earth's surface with tastes,
so the body constantly acts, being entirely the receptacle of fluids; / and smell is produced from it, and from smell taste arises again.
From that a great fire was born; look at the illustration, O lord of the earth: / just as fire comes from wood and then illuminates the wood,
even so fire arises from fluid within the body. / It constantly circulates there and nourishes the body, O lord of the earth.
As long as there is an excess of fluid, so long does the living soul remain calm; / having acted in that manner, the fire remains in the form of hunger.
Fierce, it desires food together with water; / and it receives the gift of food and water, O lord of the earth.
The fire consumes blood, and likewise semen, without a doubt; / from that arises consumption, the destroyer of the entire body.
When there is an excess of fluid, O king, then the fire is not calmed; / but afflicted by fluid, it arises in the form of fever.
Obstructing the neck, the back, the hips, the anus, and all the joints, / the fire stands; the fire rages in the body.
Its excess constantly moves and nourishes the body on all sides; / but fluid attains fixation, and then takes the form of strength.
Excessive through strength alone, it agitates the vital spots from semen; / through that very thing desire is born, which becomes like a dart, O king.
That is declared to be the fire of desire, which destroys strength, O king; / through addiction to copulation, destruction occurs in the body.
Afflicted by the fire of desire, a creature takes refuge in a woman; / stupified through addiction to copulation, emaciated by desire,
the body becomes bereft of radiance, and loss of strength occurs. / When he becomes weak, rendered feeble, impelled by fire,
that fire consumes the blood and semen in the body; / through the destruction of semen and blood, the body becomes empty.
Wind arises, exceedingly fierce and of terrifying appearance; / then he becomes discolored, tormented by pain, with an empty mind.
His mind wanders constantly, fixed upon whatever woman he has seen or heard of; / no satisfaction arises in the body, as the path of his mind remains greedy.
Ugliness and beauty arise in the midst of contemplation; / when the lustful man becomes bereft of strength through the wasting of flesh and blood,
gray hair appears in the body destroyed by the fire of desire; / because of that, the lustful man, having become aged day by day, is born [thus].
As he thinks of a woman during sexual intercourse like a usurer [thinks of his money], / just so does the loss of his vitality occur, O lord of men.
From that the body is born, and it attains the nature of destruction; / fire is produced again in the form of old age, without a doubt.
In the form of consumption of living beings, a terrible fever arises; / all immobile and mobile beings are tormented by fever.
Tormented by many afflictions, they all go to destruction. / All this has been related to you; what else shall I say to you?
Addressed thus, the great king spoke these words to Mātali:

2.65.m: Yayāti said: / The body is the protector of dharma together with the self, O Mātali; / it does not go to heaven—tell me the reason for that.
Mātali said: / There is no permanent union even of the five elements, O lord of the earth; / they exist with the self, but do not [remain] five by union.
An aggregate of them all exists in the village of the body; / tormented by old age, they all go to their respective places.
Just as the earth, O great king, is made abundant in moisture, / and dampened by moistures the earth attains softness, O lord of the earth,
and is pierced by ants and mice, / and holes and large-bellied anthills arise,
so scrofula and eczema arise in the body; / and being pierced by worms, this body, O best of men,
produces abdominal tumours then, which cause immediate pain. / Connected with these faults, O son of Nahuṣa, / how can this body go to heaven through union with the vital breath, O lord of men?
This earthy portion in the body is established for a temporary purpose; / the body does not go to heaven, but remains just as the earth does.
All this has been related to you concerning what belongs to the earth through multitudes of faults.

2.66.m: Yayāti said: / This body falls through sin, and [also] through dharma; listen, Mātali: / I do not see any distinction even for merit upon the earth.
The body is born again just as was its previous fall. / How is the body produced? Tell me that in detail.
Mātali said: / Now, for men residing in hell, a body arises from the elements in a single moment / through adharma alone.
Likewise, through dharma alone, an apparitional, divine body / is immediately produced for the gods from the essence of the elements.
The body of great souls, which is caused by mixed action, / is to be known as fourfold through the transformation of its form:
the plant-born are to be known as immobile, consisting of grass, shrubs, and the like; / worms, insects, moths, and the like are the bodies born of sweat;
the egg-born are all birds, snakes, and crocodiles, O lord of the earth; / and the womb-born are to be known as humans and four-footed beasts.
There, the earth moistened with water, cooked by heat in the blood, / and blown by wind, receives the seed in the field.
Just as seeds that are sown, when sprinkled again with water, / attain softness and proceed to the state of having roots,
and from that root comes the emergence of a shoot, from the shoot the production of a leaf, / from the leaf a stalk, then a stem, and from the stem production occurs again,
and from that production milk appears, and from milk the production of grain, / and from grain, when cooked, the medicinal plants thus arise;
seventeen are remembered as the best, beginning with barley and ending with rice, / plants rich in the essence of fruit; the remaining are proclaimed to be inferior.
These, reaped and crushed, previously prepared by sages / with winnowing baskets, mortars, vessels, and the like, with cooking pots, water, and fires,
undergo transformation sixfold according to their specific varieties, / attaining manifold tastes through mutual combination of flavors:
chewable, edible, drinkable, lickable, suckable, and crunchable, O lord of the earth; / their divisions have six members, and their qualities are six, beginning with sweet.
That food, eaten in lumps and morsels by embodied beings, / sequentially establishes all the vital breaths in the fundamental receptacle of food.
That wind divides the undigested food that was consumed into two parts; / entering into the midst of the food, it cooks it and separates its constituents.
Having placed the water above the fire, and that food above the water, / the prāṇa itself, standing below the water, gently fans the fire.
Fanned by the wind, the fire makes the water very hot; / by conjunction with the heat, that food is then thoroughly cooked on all sides.
That which is cooked becomes twofold: the waste separately, and the chyle separately. / The waste, separated into twelve excretions, passes out from the body:
Ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, lips, genitals, and anus / secrete wastes; sweat, feces, and urine are remembered as twelve.
All the channels are connected completely to the lotus of the heart; / at their openings the prāṇa deposits that subtle chyle.
With that chyle the prāṇa again fills those channels; / filled, those channels nourish the body on all sides.
Then, situated within the channels, that chyle is cooked / by the bodily heat; and being cooked, a twofold digestion occurs again.
Skin, flesh, bone, marrow, fat, and blood are produced; / from blood arise body hairs and flesh, and from flesh hair and sinew.
From sinew arises marrow, and bones; adipose tissue arises from marrow and bone; / through the agency of marrow arises transformation, and semen consisting in procreation.
Thus the twelve transformations of the peaceful one are proclaimed; / semen is its transformation, and from semen arises the body.
When, during the fertile period, defectless semen is deposited in the womb, / it, joined with wind, attains unity with the woman's blood.
At the moment of emission of semen, the soul, accompanied by its causal body, / constantly enters the womb, constrained by its own actions.
Along with the blood, the semen becomes an embryo in one day; / in five nights, bubbliness arises in that embryo.
In merely a month, fleshiness is produced fivefold: / the neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, and the belly.
The hands and feet, the two sides, the waist, and the body: / in two months the joints arise in due order.
In three months hundreds of sprouting joints are produced; / in four months the fingers and so forth appear in sequence.
The mouth, nose, and ears are produced in five months; / the row of teeth and the tongue arise, and further the nails.
Within six months the holes in the two ears are formed; / and the anus, penis, vulva, and member are also produced.
The joints that are in the body are formed in seven months; / it is complete with major and minor limbs, and endowed with head-hair.
In the eighth month its limbs become distinctly differentiated; / endowed with the five elements, it remains fully matured.
By the strength of the mother's food, and by the sixfold flavor / attached through the umbilical cord, it grows day by day.
Then, complete in this body, the soul attains memory: / it recognizes pleasure, pain, sleep, dream, and past deeds.
"I have died and was born again; I was born and have died again; / thousands of diverse wombs have been seen by me in many ways.
Now, as soon as I am born and have received initiation, / I will accomplish what is beneficial, so that there will be no origin in a womb again."
Remaining in the womb, it reflects thus: "When I have emerged from the womb, / I will study supreme knowledge, which turns back mundane existence."
Severely tormented of necessity by the great misery of the womb, / the soul, dwelling subject to karma, contemplates the means of liberation.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain stands in agony, / so the embodied being, enclosed in the membrane of the womb, remains in grief, distressed.
Just as one fallen into the ocean stays in agony, agitated, / so, with its limbs drenched by amniotic fluid, it remains agitated in mind.
Just as someone placed in an iron pot is cooked by fire, / so, cast into the pot of the womb, it is cooked by the digestive fire.
Whatever pain is produced for one whose body is incessantly pierced with fire-hot needles, / eight times that pain exists in the womb.
Nowhere is there a residence more painful than dwelling in a womb; / it is an incomparable, most dreadful distress and narrow confinement for embodied beings.
Thus has this suffering in the womb indeed been proclaimed for living beings, / for all moving and stationary beings, according to their own wombs.
Ten million times greater than that of the womb is the agony from the crushing of the birth passage / that occurs for the embodied soul being born, who is rendered senseless,
crushed like sugar cane, ground by the mallet of sin, / being expelled from the womb by the violent winds of childbirth.
A very great sorrow arises, and he finds no protection. / Just as sugarcanes, when pressed by a machine, are drained of their sap,
so the body in the womb is cast down by the pressure of the [birth-]machine— / an osseous, rounded form wound about with sinewy bonds,
smeared with blood, flesh, and fat, a receptacle for substances like feces and urine, / covered with hair, body hairs, and nails, the ultimate abode of disease,
having the mouth as a single large entrance, adorned with eight windows, / with the two lips as doors, and furnished with teeth, tongue, and throat,
with a stream of sweat through the channels, overflowing with phlegm and bile, / seized by old age and sorrow, situated in the fire of Time's mouth,
assailed by lust and anger, pounded by breaths, / afflicted with the thirst for pleasure, hidden, obedient to the power of attachment and aversion,
with each and every limb covered, wrapped in the chorion, / emerged through the narrow, unseparated passage of the birth canal,
with limbs steeped in feces, urine, and blood, arisen from the six sheaths; / an assembly forming a cage of bones is to be recognized in this body:
three hundred [bones] and a hundred more, and five hundred muscles, / covered completely with thirty-five million hair follicles,
a body supplied with tens of millions of these fleshy channels, / coarse and subtle, visible and ultimately invisible.
Through these there is impure perspiration, and they dwell inside; / thirty-two teeth are declared, and twenty nails are remembered,
a kuḍava of bile should be known, and likewise half an āḍhaka of phlegm, / and five palas of fat, and half of that of lymph,
five palas of tumors are known, ten palas of adipose tissue, / three palas of arterial blood, and marrow is four times the blood,
half a kuḍava of semen should be known, and half of that is the vitality of embodied beings; / and the meat in a lump is said to be a thousand palas,
the blood is to be known as a hundred palas, and feces and urine are beyond measure. / Thus, O king, there is the perpetual dwelling of the self in the house of the body,
which is impure, while [the self] is pure, fashioned by the bondage of karma; / from the union of semen and menstrual blood, the body is born somewhere,
perpetually conjoined with feces and urine; therefore it is remembered as impure. / Just as a jar filled with excrement inside and outside [is never] clean,
even when cleansed with purification, this body remains impure. / Contacting which even extremely pure things like the five cow-products and oblations
quickly reach impurity; therefore this body is impure. / Contacting which even delightful and fragrant foods and drinks
quickly reach impurity; what else could be impure after that? / O people, why do you not see that which goes out day by day?
The filth accompanying the body is putrid; how can its vessel be clean? / Even when cleansed with the five cow-products and kuśa-water,
the body does not attain purity, just like a charcoal being rubbed. / He whose streams flow continually like those of a mountain,
composed of impurities beginning with phlegm and urine—how is that body cleansed? / For the body, which is a reservoir of all impurities, there is
not even a single clean part, nor can it become clean even with [cleansing]. / If by day or if by night the hand is washed with earth and water,
even so it does not possess purity; yet men do not become detached from it! / Even when diligently adorned with supreme incenses and the like,
this body does not abandon its innate nature, just like a bent dog's tail. / Just as black wool by its very nature never becomes white,
so even when purified, the bodily form cannot become stainless. / Even while smelling its own foul odor, even while seeing its own filth,
this world does not feel revulsion, even while pinching its nose! / Ah, the greatness of delusion, by which the world is thoroughly blinded!
Smelling and seeing the faults of its own body, it does not become detached. / If a man does not feel revulsion from the bad odor of his own body,
what other cause for detachment can be taught to him? / The entire world is pure indeed; only the body is utterly impure,
by touch of a part of whose filth even a clean person becomes impure. / Purification of the body is proclaimed for removing the odor and the smearing;
after the departure of both, one is purified by purity of inner disposition. / Even with all the water of the Gaṅgā and loads of earth smeared upon the limbs,
a mortal of foul-smelling body who is corrupted in disposition is not cleansed. / A wicked-minded person is not cleansed by bathing in sacred fords and by austerities;
one's bodily form washed at a sacred ford does not attain purity. / For one whose inner disposition is corrupted, even if he enters fire,
there is neither heaven nor liberation, only the burning of the body. / Purity of inner disposition is the supreme cleansing, the authority in all rituals:
A beloved wife is embraced with one disposition, a daughter with another; / the mental disposition differs even regarding identical objects.
In one way indeed does a virtuous woman think of her son, in another way of her husband; / according as one's nature is, O fortunate one, it has been explained.
Even when embraced, a man would not consort with a wife who is devoid of feeling; / he would not eat various foods, though flavorful and fragrant,
without desire; therefore, inner disposition is the cause in all matters. / Purify the mind with effort; what use are other, external cleansings?
Clean through inner disposition, the purified soul finds heaven and liberation. / Moreover, with the spotless water of knowledge and the earth of dispassion,
the stain of feces and urine of ignorance and passion would be destroyed by purifications. / Thus indeed they know this body to be impure by nature;
one should know it to be worthless and void of substance, like the core of a plantain tree. / Having known the body to be full of faults in this way, the wise man who becomes detached from it
transcends saṃsāra, [while] one of firm grasping remains [bound]. / Thus this great hardship, the sorrow of birth, has been declared.
Due to the fault of ignorance of men and under the sway of various karmas, / whatever understanding one had while in the womb is destroyed once born,
for the embodied being is deeply swooned by the pain from the pressure of the birth canal, / and by the external wind, through association with delusion.
As soon as he is touched by that dread [wind], a fever arises; / through that great fever, a great delusion is produced.
For one deeply bewildered, loss of memory quickly arises again; / from that loss of memory, and under the sway of past karma,
pleasure arises for that creature in that very birth. / Attached and deluded, this world engages in wrong action,
and knows neither the self, nor the supreme, nor the deity; / it hears not the highest good, and though having eyes, it sees not.
Going slowly on a level path, it seems to stumble at every step; / though intellect is present, it does not understand even when instructed by the wise.
Thereby a man, obedient to the sway of greed, suffers in saṃsāra. / And in the absence of memory of the womb, the scripture was spoken by Śiva
in order to recount that sorrow, effecting heaven and liberation. / Since, even when that auspicious [teaching] that accomplishes dharma, pleasure, and wealth is known,
they do not work out their own highest good, that is a great wonder here. / Moreover, in childhood there is great sorrow because the senses and intellect are unmanifest;
even though wishing, one unable to do good deeds cannot speak or act. / The emergence of teeth is a great sorrow, as is [that caused] by restlessness and wind,
and affliction by various childhood diseases and childhood spirits; / his limbs overcome with thirst and hunger, he stays in one place or wanders about.
A child, through delusion, engages in eating feces, urine, and the like; / in boyhood, [there is misery] through ear-piercing and through beatings by father and mother,
and through studying the alphabet and so forth under the discipline of teachers and others; / and when the function of the senses is uncontrolled, for one afflicted by lust and passion,
constantly distressed by disease, whence indeed can there be happiness in youth? / Through envy very great misery arises, and from delusion misery is produced.
There, for one who is angered, passion leads solely to misery; / exhausted by the fire of desire, he finds no sleep at night.
Or by day, whence is there happiness, due to anxiety over acquiring wealth? / The drops of semen of a man whose body is fatigued over women—
they are not to be regarded as for happiness, like drops born of sweat. / For a leper and a base man afflicted with worms,
the pleasure that comes from scratching and the heat of fire—such they know [pleasure] in women to be. / What is considered happiness through anxiety over acquiring wealth,
the same should be understood regarding women; there is nothing more. / That very suffering of a mortal without which there is relief of mind—
that mutual [delight] formerly attained, becomes in the end quite otherwise. / Thus, what is seized by old age, permeated by sickness, is not pleasing.
Seeing oneself oppressed by old age as if by something unprecedented, / who, not becoming detached, is more unconscious than that?
Even a creature overcome by old age is humiliated by wife, sons, and kinsmen, / and because of weakness, by servants of wicked conduct.
Joined with old age, one is not able to accomplish dharma, wealth, pleasure, / or liberation; therefore, while young, one should practice dharma.
An imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and the rest is called disease; / this body is proclaimed as a collection of wind and the rest.
Therefore, this body of the soul is to be known as consisting of disease, / because it is not distinct from wind and the rest, and is a cage of diseases.
Through diseases of various kinds, the embodied being undergoes many forms of pain; / and those must be known by oneself—what else shall I say?
One hundred and one deaths are established in this body; / among them one is conjoined with natural time, and the rest are remembered as accidental.
Those that are declared here to be accidental are alleviated by medicines, / prayers, burnt offerings, and gifts; but timely death is not alleviated.
If there were no untimely death, a person would eat without suspicion of tasting poison; / and because he does not eat it, he fears untimely death.
Various diseases there, as well as creatures like serpents, / poisons and black magic spells are the gateways of death for embodied beings.
Even Dhanvantari himself cannot restore to health / one afflicted by all diseases who has reached his time; nor can it happen otherwise.
Neither medicine, nor austerity, nor donation, nor a mother, nor kinsmen / are able to deliver a man afflicted by time.
By great souls perfected in elixirs, austerity, recitations, and yoga / an intermediate pacification may occur, yet one will reach timely death.
Having died, he is born again among womb-worms by force of karma; / he who would see separation through dissolution of the body due to the exhaustion of karma—
that is designated as death, not absolute destruction in the highest sense. / For one entered into great darkness, when the vital spots are severed,
there is no comparison anywhere here to the pain in the death of a creature. / 'Ah, father! Mother! Beloved!' he cries out thus in deep distress.
Just as a frog [is seized] by a serpent, the world is swallowed by death. / Abandoned by his kinsmen, though surrounded by loved ones,
breathing long and hot with a parched mouth, / turning over on his bed, he faints again and again.
Utterly bewildered, he violently throws his hands and feet to and fro; / from the bed he desires the ground, from the ground the bed, then the earth again.
Helpless and stripped of shame, smeared with urine and feces, / and begging for water, his throat, lips, and palate dry,
thinking of his own wealth: 'Whose will these be when I am dead?' / being led away by the messengers of Yama, dragged by the noose of time,
he dies right as they watch, his throat rattling. / The soul, like a leech, gradually enters from body to body;
it attains the subsequent limb and abandons the former body. / For the discerning, the suffering from begging is indeed greater than from death.
In death the pain is momentary; caused by begging it is endless. / Even Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, became a dwarf because of asking.
Who else could be greater than him, who will not incur humiliation? / This has now been known by me, which is heavier than death:
one should not beg further from another; craving is the cause of humiliation. / There is sorrow at the beginning, so too sorrow in the middle, and dreadful sorrow at the end.
By the nature of all beings, such is the succession of sorrows. / As for these sorrows, whether present or past,
a man should not grieve for birth, nor indeed does he turn away from it. / From eating too much comes great sorrow; from eating too little, the same thereupon.
The throat tears while eating; and where is happiness in eating? / For hunger is traditionally known as the foremost disease among all sicknesses.
It is pacified only for an instant by the balm of medicine that is wholesome food. / The pain of the disease of hunger is severe, cutting down all strength;
overcome by it, a man dies, just as from other diseases. / And what happiness is there in its taste, turning on the tip of the tongue?
From that moment, in half the time, having reached the throat it ceases. / Thus, food is regarded as medicine for those burning with the disease of hunger;
it should not be considered by the wise as true happiness in the highest sense. / And he who lies down like a dead man, devoid of all activity—
where is happiness even there, for one whose mind is driven by darkness? / And what happiness is there upon waking, for one whose mind is afflicted by duties,
by great weariness through agriculture, trade, servitude, cattle-rearing, and the like; / in the morning by urine and feces; at noon by hunger and thirst?
Satisfied, creatures are troubled by desire, and at night by sleep. / There is sorrow in acquiring wealth, and sorrow in guarding what has been acquired;
sorrow in loss, and sorrow in spending; where indeed is the happiness of wealth? / From thieves, from waters, from fire, from one's own people, and from the king,
there is constant fear for the wealthy, as fear of death is for embodied beings. / Just as in the air meat is eaten by birds, on earth by beasts of prey,
and in water it is eaten by fish, so is the rich man everywhere. / [Riches] delude in times of fortune, and they obstruct in adversity;
they cause distress at the time of earning; when could riches bring happiness? / Formerly, a wealthy man was anxious; afterwards, he was free from desire for all wealth.

Between the two, the wealthy man was sorrowful; I consider the one with a detached mind to be happy. / Through the heat of spring and summer, through the fierce [cold] during the seasonal junctures of rain,
and by wind, sun, and rain, where is happiness even in time? / There is sorrow in the elaborateness of marriage, and again in bearing the womb thereof,
and sorrow through the difficulties of childbirth, and sorrow from cleaning feces and such; / in the disease of a son's teeth or eyes: 'Alas, what misery! What shall I do?
The cows are lost, the farming is ruined, and my wife has run away; / these guests have arrived at my house, heralding fear for me;
my wife has young children; who will do the cooking? / At the time of my daughter's marriage, what kind of groom will there be?'
For householders overwhelmed by such worries, where is happiness?
For a man distressed by family worries, his sacred learning, conduct, and all good qualities / perish together with his body, like water poured into an unbaked jar.
Where is happiness even in sovereignty, with anxiety over peace and war? / Where there is fear even of one's son, what kind of happiness is there indeed?
For almost all embodied beings there is fear of their own kind, / because of desiring the same object, just as between dogs.
No king renowned on the surface of the earth, entering a forest, / having disregarded everything, remains happily free from fear.
In battle, indeed, the valiant son of a sage threw down to the earth / the thousand arms of the illustrious Kārtavīrya.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, struck down the peerless, soaring prowess / of that very great-souled Rāma, the sage's son.
By Jarāsandha, the glory of Rāma was destroyed with his splendor; / of Jarāsandha, by Bhīma; and of him, by the son of Pavana.
Even Hanumān was hurled by the sun and fell to the ground. / Arjuna, who had slain all the Nivātakavacas, the Dānavas arrogant with power,
that glorious Arjuna was utterly defeated by cowherds. / The sun, though endowed with brilliance, is sometimes covered by clouds;
the cloud is scattered by the wind; the wind's power is conquered by mountains; / the mountains are burned by fire; that fire is extinguished by water;
that water is dried up by suns; those suns, together with the water / and all three worlds, perish on the day of Brahmā.
Brahmā too, along with the thirty [gods], is again withdrawn / at the end of the period of two parārdhas by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Thus in worldly existence there is no power whatever that is supreme over all, / setting aside the one Lord of the universe, the imperishable Supreme Self.
Knowing that everything has something superior to it, one should abandon excessive pride. / In such a world as this, who is a god, or who is a wise man?
For no one is all-knowing, nor is anyone a fool in every respect; / to whatever extent one knows, to that extent he is wise in that matter.
In calm equipoise, however, power is considered equal everywhere; / because of the superiority of wealth, someone's power is seen somewhere.
The gods were conquered by the Dānavas; they were conquered again by the gods; / thus the world is mutually dependent through fates of victory and defeat.
In this way, for kings, a pair of garments, a single prastha of food and water, / a vehicle, a bed, and a seat [suffice]; the rest is merely for sorrow.
Even in a seven-storied mansion, occupancy is merely a single bed; / from thousands of water-jars there is only an increase in trouble and effort.
At dawn, the blare of musical instruments sounds the same for the city-dwellers [as for a king]; / in kingship there is indeed only pride: "This is being played in my house."
Every ornament is a burden; every ointment is dirt; / all singing is mere prattle; dancing is the behavior of a madman.
Thus, upon reflection, where is happiness from the enjoyments of kingship? / Kings have anxiety in war, or through mutual desire for victory.
Generally, from the intoxication and arrogance of fortune, great kings like Nahuṣa / reached heaven and fell down; who obtains happiness through fortune?
And whence can there be happiness even in heaven, seeing another's blazing fortune / positioned progressively higher, of gods excelling one another?
In heaven, the fruit of merit is enjoyed by men with the cutting of its root; / and no other action is performed: that is a very terrible fault there.
Just as a tree with its roots severed falls to the ground in time, / so the dwellers of heaven fall down upon the exhaustion of merit.
For those intent on desiring happiness, amidst the floods of experiencing pleasure, / sorrow suddenly falls upon the dwellers of heaven—what misery in heaven!
Thus, upon reflection, there is no happiness even in heaven for the gods; / for there is exhaustion when objects of desire are attained, and [heavenly existence] is for the enjoyment of past actions.
There is great, terrible suffering for embodied beings in the fires of hell, / through terrible and diverse states arising from speech, mind, and body:
Severe cutting by axes and the stripping of barks, / and the falling of leaves, branches, and fruits by violent wind;
Through uprooting by rivers, elephants, and other embodied creatures, / and through forest fires, frost, and drying up, there is sorrow among immobile species.
Likewise, for snakes and serpents there is terrible suffering in anger, / the slaughter of the venomous in the world, and binding with a snare.
For insects, there is sudden birth and death again and again; / thus there are many kinds of sorrows for the groups of crawling creatures.
For beasts, there is slaughter of themselves and striking with sticks, / terror through piercing the nose, and severe whipping with a goad;
Binding of the limbs with canes, wooden fetters, and a hook; / mental distress in their disposition, and affliction by beggars, young men, and others;
Through separation from their own herds, and forcible leading and tethering, / in this way there are manifold sorrows for the bodies of beasts.
From rain, cold, and heat there is very grievous suffering for birds seized [in traps]; / thus there are many kinds of sorrows for the bodies of those undergoing torment.
For men, there is great suffering in living in the womb, and likewise suffering in birth, / the sorrow and ignorance of early childhood, and the discipline of the teacher in youth;
In young adulthood, sorrow from desire and passion, and again from jealousy; / through agriculture, trade, servitude, and activities such as tending cattle;
And in old age, through affliction by decrepitude and diseases; / in dying there is great suffering, and in supplication even greater than that.
There is great fear from the king, fire, clouds, lightning, thieves, and enemies; / there is fear in acquiring and guarding wealth, and again in its loss and spending.
Miserliness, envy, pride, and great fear when wealth increases, / and engagement in what should not be done are constant sorrows for the rich.
Livelihood as a servant, usury, servitude, dependence on others, / union with the desirable and undesirable, and unions by the thousands;
Famine, misfortune, foolishness, and poverty, / degradation of status, hellish torment, and the oppressive power of the king;
The sorrow of mutual defeat, great fear from one another, / and mutual rage: such is the suffering of a king and of sovereigns.
The impermanence of all states here for the embodied being whose desires are artificial; / and through mutually piercing the vitals, and mutually oppressing with taxes;
Greedy through distinction of sin, and devouring of one another— / since the moving and unmoving world is frightened by such sorrows,
Therefore a wise person should renounce everything, from hell up to humankind. / Just as one carrying a burden from shoulder to shoulder considers it relief,
So in this world all sorrow is only appeased by sorrow. / The floods of sensory enjoyment are always accompanied by mutual rivalry.
And from the exhaustion of merit, sorrow is fixed for the gods in heaven; / birth occurs in thousands of various wombs through the decay of merit.
Diseases of various kinds are remembered even in the world of the gods: / for the head of the Sacrifice was severed and joined again by the two Aśvins;
Due to that fault, there is always a head ailment for the Sacrifice; / and leprosy for the sun Mārtaṇḍa, and dropsy for Varuṇa;
Defect of teeth for Pūṣan, paralysis of the arm for the husband of Śacī; / and a very great wasting disease is proclaimed for Soma;
And there was a very great fever even for Dakṣa Prajāpati; / and in kalpa after kalpa, there is destruction even of the great gods;
At the end of the time of two parārdhas, there is impermanence even of Brahmā. / Furthermore, Brahmā lusted after Dakṣa's daughter and granddaughter;
And through wrath the lord cursed the goddess Jayā who knew yoga. / Wherever desire and anger abide, there are the faults made of them;
And all sorrows are present there without doubt. / Dispersed birth and death, and omnivorousness for the consumer of oblations;
The slaying of a woman, attachment to desire, and charioteership in the Pāṇḍava army; / Tripura was burned by Rudra, and the sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed;
The birth of Skanda from semen, and thousands of playthings and the like— / in this way, even the three gods are endowed with faults such as passion.
Beyond these is the Lord, tranquil, complete, the giver of liberation. / In this way, this entire universe stands in mutual competition.
Knowing it to be agitated by sorrows, one should attain supreme world-weariness; / and from world-weariness there would be dispassion, and from dispassion the arising of knowledge.
Through knowledge one would attain that supreme knowledge, auspicious liberation; / freed from all sorrow, established in oneself, one is then happy;
All-knowing and complete, he is called liberated. / Mātali said: / All this has been declared to you, which was asked by you.
Discrimination between dharma and adharma is indeed the source of all knowledge. / I must go forward to the world of Indra by the command of the king of gods.

2.67.m: Yayāti said: / Through the occasion of my good fortune, my sight of you / has occurred, O charioteer of Śakra; this is an incomparable blessing for me.
Humans in the mortal world commit terrible sin; / tell me now, O Mātali, the ripening of their actions.
Mātali said: / Let it be heard; I shall declare the characteristic of sinful conduct, / upon hearing which, great knowledge arises in this world.
Those who revile the Veda, and revile the conduct of Brahmā— / that should be known as a great sin even by those wise in knowledge.
He who would indeed inflict harm on all virtuous people / commits a great sin indeed, and would not pass beyond it even by expiation.
And abandoning the conduct of their family, they adopt other conduct; / and this is declared to be a terrible sin by those who know proper duty.
Reviling mother and father, striking sisters, / and reviling the father's sister—that is surely a sin.
When the time for a śrāddha has arrived, passing over a son-in-law / or a daughter's son who resides within five krośas,
passing over a sister or a sister's son, one acts, / feeding someone else out of lust, anger, or fear—
the ancestors do not eat [it], nor do the gods eat [it]; / and this sin committed by him is equal to slaying his father.
When the time for giving gifts has arrived, after a brāhmaṇa has approached, / passing over a lavish gift, it is given only to a few;
a gift is given to one and not given to the others: / this is considered a dreadful sin that causes gifts to fail.
Abandoning one's own brāhmaṇas who abide in service in the sacrificer's house, / whatever gift [is given] does not have the characteristics of a [proper] gift.
A vipra endowed with virtuous conduct who has taken refuge [with one]— / him one should support well by every means, with many excellent gifts, O king.
