One should not calculate whether he is a fool or a learned man; a vipra is always to be maintained, / endowed with all merits, with many excellent gifts, O king.
Honoring him, the learned man, one should always revere a vipra who has arrived; / if, abandoning him, one gives a gift to another brāhmaṇa,
his giving and his offering in fire become fruitless, there is no doubt about this. / A brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, and a śūdra as the fourth—
at all auspicious times, one should honor the dvija who has taken refuge [with him], / whether he is a fool or learned; hear the meritorious fruit of that:
the fruit of an aśvamedha sacrifice arises for him. / For what reason, O king, having the ability, would one not perform it?
If another vipra arrives at that time during the śrāddha rite, / one should then honor both of them with food and clothing,
and with betel and sacrificial gifts; his ancestors will be delighted. / After the śrāddha feast is eaten, a gift and sacrificial fee should always be given;
if the performer of the śrāddha does not give, it becomes equal to cow-slaughter and the like. / Therefore, one should honor both of them with faith, O best of kings.
Or, on account of poverty, one may honor just that one. / When Vyatīpāta has arrived, or Vaidhṛti, O best of kings,
and on the new moon, O king, on the anniversary of death, or in the other fortnight [of the ancestors], / thus a śrāddha should be performed by the three castes beginning with the brāhmaṇa.
In a sacrifice, O great king, one should employ priests; / likewise, vipras should always be employed for the gifts of a śrāddha.
An unknown brāhmaṇa should never be employed by a prudent man; / but one whose lineage and family through three generations are known,
as well as his conduct, O king—such a vipra one should invite. / If his family is not known, one should discern [him] by his conduct.
When a śrāddha-gift is to be performed, even a fool is pure [if his conduct is known], / but an unknown vipra may be [even] one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs.
The śrāddha-gift is to be performed, therefore one should invite that [known] vipra; / but hospitality to an unfamiliar guest should be performed [separately], O best of kings.
If a sinner acts otherwise, he surely goes to hell. / Therefore, a vipra should be employed at gifts, at a śrāddha, and on sacred days.
One should examine the vipra first, and [then] employ him in a śrāddha and in gifts. / The ancestors do not eat in his house if deprived of a vipra;
having uttered a curse, they then depart from a śrāddha devoid of vipras. / He becomes a great sinner, even if he were equal to Brahmā.
Whoever, abandoning the conduct of his fathers, lives [otherwise], O best of men, / is to be known as a great sinner, excluded from all dharmas.
Those who abandon the conduct of Śiva and of Viṣṇu which bestows enjoyment, / and revile brāhmaṇas and dharma, are to be known as promoters of sin.
Those who abandon the conduct of Śiva, hate devotees of Śiva, / and revile Hari—those sinners are constantly haters of the Veda;
those revilers of virtuous conduct are the greatest committers of major sins. / The prime, supreme, auspicious, sacred knowledge is the Bhāgavata [Purāṇa];
those who revere the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], the Harivaṃśa, the Matsya, the Kūrma, / or the Pādma—I shall declare their welfare:
by that person the god Madhusūdana is worshipped visibly. / Therefore one should revere the Vaiṣṇava knowledge dear to Viṣṇu.
And constantly in the house of God [should be kept] a Vaiṣṇava book, O king; / when that is worshipped, O vipra, the Lord of Kamalā is worshipped.
Without worshipping the knowledge of Hari, those who sing and write [it], / bestow it without understanding, listen to it, and recite it,
and play with it out of greed, or under the rule of false knowledge, / and place it as they please in impure locations—
one should manifest the knowledge of Hari securely and openly; / but whoever has studied and is capable, yet acts negligently,
and whoever speaks or listens to it while impure and in an impure place: / all this, in brief, is remembered as equal to reviling sacred knowledge.
He who desires to listen to the scripture without first honoring the guru, / and performs no service, but deliberately violates his command,
who does not welcome his words and gives back talk, / and who shows neglect when the guru's task is to be accomplished,
or that evildoer who abandons his guru when he is distressed, incapacitated, / departed for a foreign land, or overcome by enemies—
I shall declare the sin of him while the Purāṇa is being read: / he shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell as long as fourteen Indras rule.
Indeed, the wicked-minded one who ignores the reciting guru, / his sin too is dreadful, consigning him to hell for a long time.
And he who shows contempt toward his [guru's] wife, sons, and friends— / this great sin is to be known as equal to reviling the guru.
The killer of a brāhmaṇa, the stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the guru's bed: / these are the perpetrators of major sins, and one who associates with them is the fifth.
He who, out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed, cuts to the quick, / especially of a brāhmaṇa, is proclaimed a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who summons a destitute brāhmaṇa who is begging, / and afterward says, 'There is nothing,' is indeed a killer of a brāhmaṇa, O king.
Moreover, he who, out of pride in his learning, humiliates an indifferent / twice-born man in the midst of an assembly, is proclaimed a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
And he who exalts himself through false merits, / or opposes his guru, is remembered indeed as a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who causes an obstacle to those whose bodies are tormented by hunger and thirst / and who desire food to eat, is called a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
A slanderer of all people, intent on seeking out faults, / cruel and causing agitation, is indeed remembered as a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who seizes land previously given to gods, twice-born men, or cows, / even if it has been lost over time, is called a killer of a brāhmaṇa.
The misappropriation of a twice-born man's wealth acquired as a deposit / is to be known as equal to the murder of a brāhmaṇa; his sin is extreme.
Abandoning the agnihotra fire in the performance of the five sacrifices, / and he who gives false testimony against his parents or gurus,
causing displeasure to devotees of Śiva, eating uneatable things, / and slaughtering innocent living beings in the forest,
and setting fire to a cowpen, a forest, a town, or a village: / these dreadful sins are equal to drinking liquor.
Seizing all the possessions of the poor, another's wife, elephants, horses, / cows, land, silver, clothing, medicinal herbs, and liquid essences,
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and silk garments, / or stealing another's deposit, is remembered as equal to stealing gold.
Failing to give a maiden eligible for marriage to a suitable groom, / having intercourse with the wives of one's son or friend, or with sisters,
committing dreadful violence against a virgin, frequenting an outcaste woman, / and having intercourse with a woman of the same varṇa [illicitly] is remembered as equal to violating the guru's bed.
The sins that have been stated to be equal to major sins / are designated as pātaka; lesser than that is a minor sin.
He who, having promised wealth to a twice-born man, does not give it, / and if the vipra forgets about it there, that is equal to a minor sin.
Misappropriation of a twice-born man's property, transgression of established boundaries, / excessive pride, excessive anger, hypocrisy, ingratitude,
attachment to external sense-objects, miserliness, deceit, jealousy, / approaching another's wife, defiling a virtuous maiden,

a younger brother married before the elder, an elder brother unmarried while the younger marries, the woman by whom it is done, / giving a maiden to either of them, and performing sacrifices for them,
abandoning sons, friends, wives, and likewise one's master in their absence [of fault], / or abandoning virtuous wives and ascetics,
slaying cows, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, women, and śūdras, / destroying the trees of a Śiva temple or a sacred grove,
he who inflicts even the slightest injury on dwellers in a hermitage, / or on their servants, dependents, cattle, grain, and forest,
stealing plows, grain, or cattle; performing sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice; / selling a sacrifice, a grove, a reservoir, a wife, or offspring;
selling pilgrimages to sacred places, fasts, vows, and good deeds; / living off women's wealth; living completely off a woman's vulva;
the man who sells his own duty, describes unrighteousness [as righteousness], / speaks ill of others' faults, and looks for weaknesses in others;
coveting another's wealth and gazing upon another's wife: / these are to be known as equal to cow-killers, O son of a king.
He who alters all the scriptures, a stealer of cows, a seller of cows, / one extremely merciless toward servants, and one who torments animals,
he who speaks false words or listens to them from others, / one treacherous to his master, treacherous to his guru, deceitful, fickle, and crooked,
he who eats while abandoning his hungry wife, sons, friends, / children, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, servants, guests, and kin,
those who eat dainties alone and do not give to one who desires it: / such a one is to be known as cooking for himself alone, reviled among the knowers of the Veda.
Those who, lacking self-control, abandon rules of conduct they have taken upon themselves, / those through whom renunciation is degraded, and those who associate with drinkers of wine,
and those who do not diligently care for a cow afflicted with consumption / or distressed by thirst and hunger: they are remembered as cow-killers destined for hell.
Those engaged in all sins, violators of four-legged animals and fields, / and he who strikes virtuous men, vipras, gurus, and cows,
those who strike a blameless woman established in the station of the virtuous, / he whose entire body is bound by sloth and who sleeps repeatedly,
those who do not nourish the weak and do not search for the lost, / who torment [beasts] with excessive burdens and make them carry loads when wounded,
those engaged in all sins, who eat in [illicit] company, / and who, toward a cow with broken limbs, afflicted by wounds and disease, and tormented by hunger,
do not diligently care for her: those people are remembered as destined for hell; / and those most sinful men who crush the testicles of bulls,
and who torment calves: such men are destined for great hell. / A guest who has arrived in hope, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue,
and those who do not honor him: they indeed go to hell. / The helpless, the maimed, the poor, the child, the aged, the severely afflicted—
the fools who have no compassion for them go to the ocean of hell. / A keeper of goats and sheep, a keeper of buffaloes, a śūdra husband of an outcaste woman,
a śūdra who behaves according to the conduct of a vipra or a kṣatriya, / artisans, craftsmen, physicians, and temple priests,
servants and ministerial officials: all are destined for hell. / And he who transgresses what is prescribed and collects taxes according to his own whim,
he shall cook in hells; and he who imposes punishment uselessly. / Under whatever king the subjects are oppressed in his realm
by bribe-takers, officials, and thieves, he cooks in hells. / Those twice-born men who accept gifts from an evildoing king
go to dreadful hells, without a doubt. / Whatever sin belongs to adulterers and thieves belongs to the king
if he fails to protect; that dreadful liability falls upon the king. / And a king who, without investigation, treats a non-thief as a thief,
or again treats a thief as a non-thief, he too surely goes to hell. / [Stealing] ghee, oil, food, drink, honey, meat, spirituous liquor, fermented drink,
molasses, sugarcane, milk, vegetables, curds, roots, fruits, / grass, wood, flowers, leaves, and bronze vessels,
Shoes, umbrella, bracelets, palanquin, a soft seat, / copper, lead, tin, bell-metal, conch and other water-born items,
musical instruments, bamboo flutes, household furnishings, / wool, cotton, silk, items made of tin or lotus-fibers,
cotton, fine clothes—those who steal these out of greed, / and other such various items:
one would go swiftly to hells even by stealing small things. / Whatever it may be, taking another's property, even the size of a mustard seed,
having stolen it, a man goes to hell, there is no doubt about this. / Whether much or little, of that which has been made another's property,
having stolen it, a man goes to hell, there is no doubt about this. / By such sins as these, immediately after departure [from life],
a man assumes his former form for the torment of the body; / these, remaining in the body, go to the world of Yama by Yama's command,
being led by the terrifying messengers of Yama, intensely suffering. / For gods, animals, and humans whose minds are fixed on adharma,
Dharmarāja is remembered as the punisher with dreadful, varied tortures. / For those possessed of discipline and conduct whose minds are stained through negligence,
the guru is the punisher through expiations, and they are not seen by Yama. / For adulterers, thieves, and those of unjust dealings,
the king is declared the punisher, while Dharmarāja is [the punisher] of those who act in secret. / Therefore, one should perform expiation for sin that has been committed.
Otherwise, there is no destruction of unexperienced [karma], even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. / Whoever performs a deed himself, causes it to be done, or approves of it
by body, mind, or speech—his fruit is a downward fall. / Thus, the varieties of sin have been told in brief as threefold. Now
the varied destinies of men of sinful deeds are being described. / Thus the fruit of dharma has been told to you in detail, O king;
what else shall I tell you? Tell me that, O best of men. / The fruit of adharma has been spoken; I will tell you of dharma as well."
Having spoken thus to the king who loved all beings, / Mātali, that great-souled one, related this to him in the context of dharma.

2.68.m:
Yayāti said:
The fruit of unrighteousness has all been heard by me, O Sūta, O lord. / Tell me also the fruit of righteousness; my curiosity is to hear it.

Mātali said:
Now, because of their sins, these four kinds [of beings] go to Yama's world— / a terrifying, dreadful place—all embodied beings helpless.
Those abiding in the womb, those being born, children, youths, the middle-aged, / men, women, eunuchs, and the aged—living beings must go from here.
There the good and bad results for embodied beings are deliberated / by Citragupta and all the others, who are impartial and all-seeing.
There are no living beings who do not go to Yama's abode; / for the deed that is done must certainly be experienced; it is deliberated upon.
Those there who have done good deeds, whose minds are gentle, endowed with compassion— / those men go by an agreeable path to Yama's dwelling.
He who would give shoes and wooden sandals to brahmins, / goes happily to Yama's abode in a great aerial chariot.
By the gift of an umbrella, embodied beings travel by a shaded path; / those who give garments go clad in divine clothing.
By giving a palanquin, one would travel happily in an aerial chariot; / by giving a comfortable seat, they go happily to Yama's abode.
The maker of a pleasure-grove goes comfortably in cool shades; / those who give flower-gardens travel by a Puṣpaka aerial chariot.
A builder of a temple to the gods, of a hermitage for ascetics, / and of shelters for the destitute, travels amusing himself in the finest mansions.
And the worshipper of gods, fire, the guru, brahmins, and mother and father—
Whatever is given with faith, even very little, to brahmins, to the poor, and to the virtuous, / obtains all desired objects in the world; and the virtuous proclaim it as a gift at a śrāddha.
Through giving with faith, [even an offering] as small as the tip of a hair is to be recognized; / in the fourfold set consisting of the recipient and so forth, my faith is ever present.
From that which is always revered in faith, the fruit of that faith arises; / he who also gives dwellings to the virtuous and the destitute—
he goes, O king, to the ancestral realm of Brahmā, which fulfills every desire. / By whom even a single cowrie is given with faith to a brahmin,
he becomes a divine guest, O king, increasing the renown of the gods; / therefore, gifts must be given by those endowed with faith; the fruit thereof is certain.

2.69.m:
Mātali said:
Now, the duties spoken by Śiva are the highest teachings of the Śivadharma; / they should be known as manifold, through distinctions in the yoga of action:
free from faults such as violence, devoid of hardship and distress, / beneficial to all beings, pure, requiring slight exertion, bearing great fruit,
endowed with endless branches, rooted solely in Śiva as their foundation, / rich in the beautiful blossoms of knowledge and meditation—the eternal Śivadharmas.
Because they uphold Śiva, and because they are upheld by words spoken by Śiva, / they are remembered as the Śivadharmas, carrying one across the ocean of worldly existence.
Likewise, non-violence, patience, truthfulness, modesty, faith, sensory restraint, / giving, sacrifice, asceticism, and charity—this ten-fold practice is the means of dharma.
Now, whether these Śivadharmas are performed separately or collectively, / for those who have attained uniform taste with Śiva, only a single destination is determined.
Just as the earth is remembered as a common realm for all living beings, / so the city of Śiva is remembered as equal for the devotees of Śiva.
Just as the enjoyments of all living beings here are remembered as unequal, / according to various distinctive merits, so are the enjoyments in the city of Śiva.
And the fruit of good and evil is experienced by all embodied beings; / and the fruit of the Śivadharma alone is enjoyed there.
Whatever kind of merit one has, through the distinction of faith and the worthy recipient, / such are the pre-eminent, auspicious enjoyments known to be his in the city of Śiva.
The attainment of the place is simply equal, but the enjoyments remain peaceful; / therefore, one should perform great merit out of a desire to attain great enjoyments.
Pre-eminence over all alone is cherished by the highest gods; / there would be sovereignty over one's own enjoyments, and Śiva is the lord of the entire universe.
Some men devoted to the yoga of knowledge are liberated right there; / but others, intent upon enjoyment, return again to worldly existence.
Therefore, one wishing for complete liberation should abandon attachment to enjoyments; / detached, with a mind and self at peace, he would attain knowledge of Śiva.
And those who, with hearts directed toward the Lord, worship the Lord occasionally, / to them also the Lord grants a place in accordance with their disposition.
Those who, having their sins destroyed, worship Rudra there even once, / to them the Lord grants enjoyments in the worlds of the piśācas.
Afflicted by the weight of sorrow, all embodied beings die; / the giver of food is declared to be a giver of merit, a giver of life, and a giver of everything.
Therefore, through the gift of food, one obtains the fruit of all gifts; / whatever jewels, enjoyments, women, and vehicles exist in the three worlds,
the giver of food obtains all that fruit in this world and in the next. / He by whose food and drink a person's body is nourished and amasses merit—
half of it belongs to that giver of food, and half to the doer, without a doubt. / The body is the supreme instrument for dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
its maintenance is through food and drink; therefore, that is the means to everything. / Food is Prajāpati visibly; food is Viṣṇu, Śiva himself.
Therefore, a gift equal to food has never been nor will ever be. / Water is remembered as the life of all three worlds;
water is purifying, divine, clean, and an elixir of all tastes. / Food, drink, a horse, a cow, clothing, a bed, a sacred thread, and seats—
these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the spirits. / In this way, by the distinction of gifts, a man [goes] to the city of Dharmarāja;
since one goes with ease indeed, one should practice dharma. / But those of cruel deeds, who are devoid of sinful gifts [or good gifts],
experience severe sorrow in hell, O delight of kings; / while the givers of gifts truly experience happiness in like manner.
For those whose souls are devoted to the yoga of action, happiness would surely arise / with divine aerial chariots of immeasurable qualities that grant every desire.
That city, which is beneficial to living beings, is filled with countless [chariots], / divine like a thousand moons, or radiant as the splendor of the sun.
It is proclaimed as the world of Rudra, endowed with all virtues; / that city is celebrated for all devotees of Śiva,
and for moving and unmoving beings who die in the sacred field of Rudra. / Even for a single day, he who worships Śaṅkara with devotion,
he too goes to the abode of Śiva, how much more so one worshipping repeatedly! / Vaiṣṇavas, devotees of Viṣṇu, and those intent upon meditating on Viṣṇu—
they too go to Vaikuṇṭha, into the presence of the discus-bearing god; / and an expounder of the Veda, righteous in soul, goes to the world of Brahmā;
and the doer of meritorious deeds goes to the world of merit through good merit. / Therefore, one should constantly cultivate devotion to the Lord within one's self by the self,
or to Hari, O great king, oneself disciplined in spirit and possessing knowledge. / Therefore, by deliberating on everything, by considering the faults of one's disposition,
in this way, through the power of Viṣṇu and by distinctive action, / a man attains a place in accordance with the region and the disposition.
Thus this other [place], the great, glorious city of Śiva, has been proclaimed; / it is remembered as causing the return of embodied beings dedicated to action.
Above Śivapura is to be known the supreme Vaiṣṇava world; / Vaiṣṇava men devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu go there.
Brahmins of good conduct, the best of men, go to Brahmaloka; / all sacrificers who know the truth go to that city.
Likewise, kṣatriyas skilled in battle go to Indraloka, / and other performers of meritorious deeds go to worlds of merit.

2.70.m: Mātali said: / I shall describe the torment of Yama, exceedingly sharp and very terrible, / which all cruel sinners, killers of brahmins, endure.
In some places sinners are cooked with fierce cow-dung fire; / in other places, by lions, wolves, tigers, biting insects, and terrible bugs;
in some places by huge leeches, again in other places by pythons, / by fierce flies, and in some places by violently poisonous serpents;
and by herds of mad elephants, powerful and trampling, / and by great bulls with sharp horns that tear up the path;
and by buffaloes with great horns that torment the bodies of wicked men, / by fierce ḍākinīs, and by terrifying rākṣasas;
afflicted by great and terrible diseases, they proceed; / mounted upon a great balance, burned in a forest fire;
violently shaken by a great, furious wind, / and shattered on all sides by a rain of heavy stones;
with crashing thunders of vajras and terrible falls of meteors, / struck down by a rain of glowing embers, they proceed;
covered by a great rain of dust, gone to Yama's realm— / the men who commit sinful deeds endure terrible sin.
Thus, according to the distinction of sins, the most sinful evildoers / endure hell, which is filled with many torments.
All this discrimination between merit and sin has been related to you. / What else shall I tell you of the peerless treatise on dharma?

2.71.m: Yayāti said: / Since everything concerning dharma and adharma has been recounted by you as peerless, / even as I listen, my faith arises once again.
Tell the enumerated abodes of the worlds of the gods, / and by the occasion of whose merit which [world] is attained, O Mātali.
Mātali said: / I will explain the realm of the gods, attained through asceticism, / endowed with yoga, which bestows the enjoyment of happiness;
I shall proclaim the state of dharma acquired separately by efforts, / and the true nature of the worlds above, in due order.
There, the sovereign power of the meat-eaters is earthly and eightfold; / therefore, that of men who have immediately attained yoga is considered equal to it.
That of the rakṣases is sixteenfold, and that of earthly beings is of that sort; / thus without exception, whatever remains belongs to the power of the race.
That of the gandharvas is aerial, and all that of the yakṣas is so considered; / Indra’s [power] is composed of the five elements, great, and fortyfold.
Soma’s is divine and mental; that of the Lord of the All is elemental; / that of the Prajāpatis and Īśāna is gentle, superior in the quality of ego-consciousness;
that pertaining to Brahmā is sixty-fourfold, an excellent power of intellect; / Viṣṇu’s is rooted in primordial matter, an authority, the abode of the Absolute.
In glorious, divine Śivapura there is sovereignty granting all desires; / the sovereignty of Śiva is infinitely manifold, a great quality of the Self;
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, pure, defined by the truth, / illuminating all, subtle, incomparable, higher than the highest;
fully complete, embodying the universe, releasing the soul from bondage. / Whatever place one has attained, one’s enjoyment is of that nature;
and by the favor of the Lord, an aerial chariot equal to that comes to be. / These myriad forms of stars are seen in their crores;
these twenty-eight are thus brightly illuminated for virtuous souls. / Those who make obeisance to the Lord here and there,
through contact, curiosity, or desire, obtain that aerial chariot; / or by chanting the name of Śiva in any context,
or if one should make obeisance, there will be no destruction for him. / Such are the great destinies there in the service of Śiva.
Even by an internal act, from a state of devotion to the Lord, / the men who remember Śaṅkara, even incidentally—
matchless happiness is to be attained by them; how much more by those devoted to him! / Those whose minds are absorbed in meditation, who contemplate Viṣṇu,
go to the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu. / The Śaiva form and the Vaiṣṇava form are one single form, O best of men;
there is no difference between the two; they are one form of the Great Soul. / Homage to Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva!
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṣṇu; / the three gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, are one single manifestation.
There is no difference among the three; they are proclaimed as distinctions of the guṇas. / You are a devotee of Śiva, O king of kings, and truly a Vaiṣṇava devotee.
Therefore the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are pleased with you; / they are well pleased, granting boons because of your action, O man of good vows.
By Indra's command I have come into your presence, O honor-giver; / go to this realm of Indra, and afterwards to that of Brahmā and Maheśvara,
and go to the Vaiṣṇava realm, free from burning and dissolution, / by this divine aerial chariot that travels everywhere.
Having a divine form, therefore, enjoy delightful divine pleasures, / having mounted the aerial chariot Puṣpaka that moves with ease.
Sukarma said: / Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, Mātali then became silent / before the king, the son of Nahuṣa, Yayāti, who knows the reality of dharma.
